content.text:
I built the calendar heatmap in `/work/index.html`. It renders with no console errors. Germany's ARE consultations follow the same summer-low, winter-high cycle every year, but the timing of the yearly peak has moved. These figures are all computed in the page:

- **Winter vs summer:** weeks 1–10 averaged higher than weeks 25–35 in 12 of the 13 complete ISO years.
- **Up to 2020:** the year's highest week fell in weeks 1–13 in 7 of 8 complete years.
- **From 2021:** the highest week fell in week 40 or later in 3 of 5 complete years.
- **2021:** there was no early-year wave; the winter-to-summer ratio was 0.86, so summer was higher.

The data runs from 2012-W40 to 2026-W43. Each year's peak week has a black outline, and hovering over a cell shows its value.

```
REPORT
deliverable: index.html
requirements:
  R1: done - ISO years 2012–2026, one row each, top to bottom
  R2: done - weeks 1..N per year, N from ISO week of 28 Dec; week 53 shown for 2015, 2020, 2026
  R3: done - d3.interpolateYlOrRd from 0 to data max; legend titled "ARE consultations per 100,000 population per week"
  R4: done - weeks before 2012-W40 and after 2026-W43 are drawn as empty grey outlines, labelled "no data" in the legend
  R5: done - week ticks (1, even weeks, 53) along the bottom; year labels on the left
  R6: done - title plus a one-sentence caption whose numbers are computed from the data
assumptions:
  - Year and week are taken from the Kalenderwoche field (ISO year), not from Saison
  - Week slots that exist in the calendar but have no data are outlined; week 53 is drawn only in years that have it
  - "Winter" means ISO weeks 1–10 and "summer" weeks 25–35; caption statistics use only complete ISO years (2013–2025)
  - If a week appeared twice its values would be averaged (none were in this data)
limitations:
  - The 2020 vs 2021 split in the caption is my choice of cut-off; the counts themselves are computed
  - Rows split the winter season across two rows, so a December–February wave appears at the right end of one row and the left end of the next
  - The colour scale runs linearly to the 2022 maximum (about 3,200), so differences between low summer weeks are hard to see
```
